2027-04-05.title: Second Monday of Resurrection
2027-04-05.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: The disciples recognise the Risen Christ
2027-04-05.alt: Season of the Resurrection (Qyamta). The second week of the Resurrection begins. The Queen of Heaven (Regina Caeli) is prayed in place of the Angelus until Pentecost. The Latin Church keeps the Annunciation of the Lord today, moved from 25 March, which fell on Pesaha Thursday; the Syro-Malabar First Set gives no transfer, so follow the direction of your eparchy.
2027-04-05.verse: Then their eyes were opened, and they recognized him; and he vanished from their sight.
theo: The Easter octave is over, and the Church goes back to ordinary Mondays: to work, to school, to the market and the bus stand. The readings of this second week of the Resurrection are chosen for exactly that return. They ask what Easter looks like in a parish with quarrels, in a family with tensions, on a road walked by two tired disciples. Paul begins with a parish that had split into fan clubs. News has reached him through Chloe's household: “there are quarrels among you, my brothers and sisters. What I mean is that each of you says, ‘I belong to Paul,’ or ‘I belong to Apollos,’ or ‘I belong to Cephas,’ or ‘I belong to Christ.’” Each group had chosen its favourite preacher, and even the people who said ‘I belong to Christ’ had turned the Lord into a party badge. Paul answers with three short questions that cut through everything: “Has Christ been divided? Was Paul crucified for you? Or were you baptized in the name of Paul?” There is only one Lord who died for us and only one name into which we were baptised. Paul even thanks God that he baptised very few of them, so that no one could claim to belong to him. His task was something else: “For Christ did not send me to baptize but to proclaim the gospel, and not with eloquent wisdom, so that the cross of Christ might not be emptied of its power.” A Church that argues about its preachers has forgotten its Crucified and Risen Lord. Unity is not a matter of everyone liking the same priest or the same style; it is the fruit of looking together at the Cross and the empty tomb.

The Gospel takes us back to the evening of Easter Sunday, on the road to Emmaus. Two disciples have walked seven miles with a stranger who explained the Scriptures to them. Now they reach their village, and “he walked ahead as if he were going on.” The Risen Lord never forces his company on anyone. He waits to be invited. “But they urged him strongly, saying, ‘Stay with us, because it is almost evening and the day is now nearly over.’ So he went in to stay with them.” That prayer, Stay with us, has been on Christian lips ever since; it is the prayer of every evening and of every life that feels the light going. Then comes the moment the whole story was moving towards: “When he was at the table with them, he took bread, blessed and broke it, and gave it to them. Then their eyes were opened, and they recognized him; and he vanished from their sight.” The four verbs are the verbs of the Last Supper, and of every Holy Qurbana: he took, blessed, broke and gave. They knew him not by his face but by what he did with bread. And as soon as they knew him, he was no longer visible in the old way, because from now on he would be present to them in the breaking of the bread.

What happens next is the shape of the Christian life. “They said to each other, ‘Were not our hearts burning within us while he was talking to us on the road, while he was opening the scriptures to us?’ That same hour they got up and returned to Jerusalem.” It was night, and it was seven miles, but the burning heart cannot wait till morning. They find the community gathered, and before they can tell their news they are told: “The Lord has risen indeed, and he has appeared to Simon!” Then they share their own story: “how he had been made known to them in the breaking of the bread.” Notice the movement: away from Jerusalem in sadness, back to Jerusalem in joy; from two scattered disciples to the gathered Church around Peter. The Risen Lord heals divisions not by argument but by gathering his people at one table. Paul's quarrelling Corinthians and the two lonely disciples need the same cure. In the Syro-Malabar Holy Qurbana, after the anaphora, the priest breaks the Holy Bread and signs the Precious Blood with it, uniting them again: the Body broken and the Blood poured out are joined, because the One who died is alive. Every parish that gathers at that altar is being made one, quarrels and all.
conn: “There is one body and one Spirit… one Lord, one faith, one baptism” (Ephesians 4:4–5); Jesus prays “that they may all be one” (John 17:21).
Paul will say a few verses later, “we proclaim Christ crucified” (1 Corinthians 1:23); in Galatians, “May I never boast of anything except the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ” (Galatians 6:14).
Abraham urges the three visitors at Mamre, “do not pass by your servant” (Genesis 18:3), and entertains the Lord unawares; “some have entertained angels without knowing it” (Hebrews 13:2).
The same four actions at the feeding of the five thousand (Luke 9:16) and at the Last Supper (Luke 22:19).
Jeremiah felt the word of God “like a burning fire shut up in my bones” (Jeremiah 20:9).
Paul hands on the same early witness: “he appeared to Cephas, then to the twelve” (1 Corinthians 15:5).
altar: At every Holy Qurbana the road to Emmaus is walked again: first the Lord opens the Scriptures to us, then he takes bread, gives thanks, breaks it and gives it. He is truly present, Body and Blood, soul and divinity, under the signs of bread and wine.
The breaking of the Holy Bread after the anaphora, and its signing with the Precious Blood, proclaim the one Christ, crucified and risen. Around that one Bread a divided people is made one body.
outline: Back to an ordinary Monday after the Easter octave.
Paul and the parish of fan clubs.
The Lord who waits to be invited.
Point 3 · Known in the breaking of the bread
The burning heart runs back to the community.
Two travellers turning round in the dark and walking seven miles back with joy.
“Stay with us, because it is almost evening.”
live: Speak kindly this week to someone in your parish or family from whom you have drifted apart.
Each evening before sleep, say: Lord, stay with us, because it is almost evening.
Come to the breaking of the bread
Attend one weekday Holy Qurbana this week, and listen to the readings as the two disciples listened on the road.
Tell one person how the Lord has made himself known to you.
fathers: Where did the Lord wish to be recognised? In the breaking of bread. We are secure: we break bread, and we recognise the Lord. He did not want to be known except there, for our sake, who would not see him in the flesh but would eat his flesh. So whoever you are who believe, do not despair because you did not see him then: you have him in the breaking of the bread.

They did not know him while he explained the Scriptures, but they knew him when they gave him bread. The truth is learned not only by hearing the commandments of God but by doing them. They welcomed a stranger to their table, and found that the stranger was God.
magis: The Eucharist is called the Breaking of Bread, because Jesus used this rite as master of the table, and by this action his disciples recognised him after his Resurrection.
The Emmaus meal is the pattern of the liturgy: the Lord explains the Scriptures, then takes bread, blesses and breaks it.
Christ bestowed unity on his Church from the beginning; the Church must always pray and work to keep, strengthen and perfect it.
Divisions wound the unity of Christ's Body; they arise from human sin and must be healed by conversion and charity.
saints: Monday 5 to Saturday 10 April: the second week of the Resurrection. Sunday 11 April: the Third Sunday of Resurrection. The Latin Church keeps the Annunciation of the Lord on Monday 5 April this year (moved from 25 March, which fell on Pesaha Thursday); Syro-Malabar faithful follow the direction of their eparchy.
2027-04-05.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, risen from the dead, you walked with your disciples on the road and made yourself known to them in the breaking of the bread. Stay with us, for it is almost evening. Open the Scriptures to us, set our hearts on fire, and heal the divisions in our parishes and families, so that we may be one in you, who were crucified for us and live for ever with the Father and the Holy Spirit. Amen. Alleluia!

catechism: The Emmaus pattern of the liturgy.
kidsaint: Cleopas was one of the two disciples walking sadly to Emmaus. A stranger joined them, explained the Bible, and then broke bread at their table: it was Jesus! Cleopas ran all the way back to Jerusalem in the dark to tell the others. Lesson: when we meet Jesus, we can't keep the good news to ourselves!

term: One of the oldest names for the Holy Qurbana, used in Luke and Acts (Acts 2:42). It recalls how Jesus broke bread at the Last Supper and at Emmaus, and how the Church shares the one Bread that makes her one body.

family.explain: Two friends of Jesus were walking home, very sad. A man walked with them and explained the Bible. When they reached home they said, ‘Stay with us.’ At supper he broke the bread, and suddenly they saw: it was Jesus! He had risen! At Holy Qurbana Jesus breaks the bread for us too.
family.intention: We pray for families and parishes where people are quarrelling, that Jesus may make them one again.
family.ask: Ask: “Is there someone we should make peace with this week? How can we do it?”

illus: Two families in a parish near Changanassery had not spoken for six years after a quarrel over the parish feast committee. Each sat on a different side of the church. One Easter season the vicar asked both fathers to carry the canopy together in a small procession. They agreed only because the vicar asked. Walking side by side under the canopy, neither knew what to say. At the end one of them said quietly, ‘We were fighting about who should be in charge of a feast for the Lord, and we forgot the Lord.’ That evening the two families ate together for the first time in six years.

pm.open: Lord Jesus, risen and present among us, open the Scriptures to us and make our hearts burn within us. Stay with us. Amen. Alleluia!
share: Has Christ been divided? (1 Corinthians 1:13). Where do I take sides in a way that divides the Body of Christ?
Stay with us, because it is almost evening (Luke 24:29). Where do I need to invite the Lord into my evening?
He had been made known to them in the breaking of the bread (Luke 24:35). How do I meet the Risen Lord in the Holy Qurbana?
Were not our hearts burning within us? (Luke 24:32). When has the word of God set my heart on fire?
interc: For the unity of the Church, and especially for unity within our own Syro-Malabar Church.
For parishes and families divided by quarrels, that they may be reconciled at the one table of the Lord.
For all who walk away from the Church in sadness, that the Lord may walk with them and bring them home.
For priests, that they may open the Scriptures and break the bread with burning hearts.
For travellers and migrants on the road tonight.
pm.close: Father, your Son made himself known to his disciples in the breaking of the bread. Gather us into one around his table, heal our divisions, and send us out with burning hearts to tell what we have seen. Through Christ our Lord. Amen. Alleluia!

homily: Dear friends, the Easter octave is over and we are back to ordinary Mondays. Today's readings show what Easter looks like in ordinary life: in a parish with quarrels, and on a road walked by two tired disciples.

Paul hears that the Corinthians are divided: I belong to Paul, I belong to Apollos, I belong to Cephas. He asks: Has Christ been divided? Was Paul crucified for you? There is only one Lord who died for us, and only one name in which we were baptised.
We have our own versions of this: my priest, my group, my side of the family. Paul says: look at the Cross. When we look together at the Crucified and Risen Lord, our little parties lose their power.
In the Gospel two disciples walk to Emmaus with a stranger. At the village he seems to go on, and they beg him: Stay with us, because it is almost evening. The Lord waits to be invited.

At table he took bread, blessed and broke it, and gave it to them, and their eyes were opened. They knew him in the breaking of the bread, as we know him at every Holy Qurbana. And that same hour they ran back to Jerusalem to the gathered community.
This week, let us invite him every evening: Lord, stay with us. And let us bring one quarrel to his table, so that he may make us one. Alleluia! Amen.
kids: Children, two friends of Jesus did not recognise him on the road. But when he broke the bread at supper, they knew him! At Holy Qurbana, when the priest breaks the Holy Bread, Jesus is there for us too.
Tonight, before you sleep, say a little prayer: ‘Jesus, stay with us!’

concl: The Risen Lord heals our divisions by gathering us at one table.
He waits to be invited; let us say every evening: Stay with us.
